findings.title: Debug logging left at Error level, dumping full ID lists
findings.body: Each batch of the cleanup loops logs at Error level (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), including the entire `ids` slice. These logs fire on every run even when nothing goes wrong. With large batch sizes (e.g. 32767), they write enormous error log lines, flood logs and alerting, and add overhead. They look like leftover debugging and should be removed or lowered to Debug without the ID list.

findings.title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: The interval for all cleanup jobs went from 10 minutes to 1 minute, and the PR description does not mention or justify it. Each job still has a 9-minute timeout, so runs can now overlap or queue back to back. That means 10x more DB load for snapshots, dashboard versions, query history and the rest. This looks like a leftover debugging change.

findings.title: MaxCount cleanup can delete the wrong rows when inserts run concurrently
findings.body: The IDs are fetched with ORDER BY id DESC plus an OFFSET of MaxCount, then deleted in a separate statement outside any transaction. This already happens every batch. Concurrent inserts shift the offset between batches, so the result is no longer one consistent cut. The comment only claims under-deletion, but this offset behaviour should be considered and documented.

findings.title: Quadratic string building for SQLite IN list
findings.body: `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` rebuilds the whole string on every iteration. That is O(n^2) for batches of tens of thousands of IDs. Use a strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt instead.

findings.title: SQLite inline path keyed on configured batch size instead of actual ID count
findings.body: The check for whether to inline IDs or use placeholders looks at the configured batch size, not at how many IDs this batch actually has. The placeholder path is still correct as long as len(ids) never exceeds the batch size. Checking len(ids) instead would make the limit handling more robust.
